 Read on mobile Scan the code with your phone to have the device code phishing instructions in your pocket while you work on the computer. Print Copy link E-mail to myself Device code phishing: what it is, how to spot it and what to do if you entered a code
 Device code phishing is a scam in which an attacker gets you to type a short code on a real Microsoft sign-in page, which hands the attacker a working login to your account without your password. If you entered a code you were not expecting, tell your IT team or secure the account now, because changing the password alone does not end the access.
 By Ugnius Kiguolis Published November 1, 2026 10 min read 
 Facts checked November 1, 2026. Removal steps tested on Windows 11 (26H2) and checked against Microsoft's and the browser makers' current documentation.
 Do it yourself · free Remove device code phishing yourself 4 steps, about 12 minutes, no software needed. 
 Start the steps ↓ Our own diagram of how device code phishing works. It is not a screenshot of a real attack; our check was a reading of Microsoft's pages, not a site test. Device code phishing: summary
 Type A phishing technique that abuses Microsoft's device code sign-in; not a program 
 Risk High for work and school accounts: access to mail and files without the password, and spread to colleagues 
 Symptoms Often none. A message asks you to enter a code on a Microsoft sign-in page; later, mail you did not send or sign-ins you do not recognise 
 How to get rid of it Report to IT, revoke sign-in sessions, review sign-ins and registered devices, then change the password and MFA 
 Our check (1 November 2026) No site to test. We read Microsoft's write-up and documentation and news reports of vendor findings; we ran no kit and tested no account 
 First seen Microsoft says the Storm-2372 campaign began in August 2024; its write-up is dated 13 February 2025 
 Show 5 more facts Platform Any device with a browser; the account is the target 
 Detection No file detection, as nothing is installed. Microsoft describes hunting signals in Defender XDR and Entra ID Protection 
 Name Device code phishing 
 Evidence 0 write-ups by security sites; details still limited 
 Facts checked 1 November 2026 
 Facts checked on 1 November 2026 against Microsoft Threat Intelligence's Storm-2372 post, Microsoft Learn pages on the device authorization grant and on blocking authentication flows, and two news reports of vendor findings. We ran no phishing kit and tested no account. Steps for ordinary users are given as an order of actions because we could not read a Microsoft page with exact screens.
 What device code phishing is, in plain words
 Device code phishing abuses a real Microsoft feature. The attacker starts a sign-in on their own machine, receives a short code from Microsoft, and persuades you to type that code on the genuine Microsoft device login page. When you finish, Microsoft treats you as having approved the attacker's session, and the attacker receives access and refresh tokens for your account.
 1 The feature being abused
 Microsoft's identity platform supports the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant. It exists so that a device without a good keyboard or browser, such as a smart TV, a printer or another input-constrained device, can have its user finish the sign-in on a phone or PC. The device shows a short user code and a web address, and the user signs in on another device. Microsoft's documentation says the user has 15 minutes from the moment the request is made, which is the default lifetime of the code.
 2 The trick
 The attacker plays the part of the input-constrained device. They request a code, then send it to you with a believable story. You open the real page, type the code, and sign in with your password and your second factor. Nothing on that page is fake. The only lie is the story that made you type the code, so the usual advice to check the web address of the sign-in page does not protect you.
 3 What the attacker gets
 Once you approve, the attacker's waiting session receives an access token and, depending on what was requested, a refresh token. A refresh token can be used to obtain new access tokens, so it can keep working long after the first one expires. The attacker never needs your password, and the multi-factor step you passed was spent on their session.
 4 Is it a vulnerability?
 No. Microsoft states in its February 2025 write-up that the technique is not a flaw in its products. It is a misuse of a feature working as designed, which is why the defence is partly policy (limit or block the flow) and partly people (do not enter codes you did not ask for).
 What it is A phishing technique, not a program. There is nothing on your device to uninstall Where it happens On the Microsoft sign-in side: the account is what is compromised, not the computer Platform Any: it works from a PC, Mac or phone browser, because the attack targets the account What is stolen Access and refresh tokens that give the attacker the same access you have Password needed? No. The attacker never learns it Code lifetime About 15 minutes by default, per Microsoft Learn Not the same as A fake login page that collects passwords, or malware that logs keystrokes How to tell the device code phishing message is fake
 How to spot it before you type anything
 You can stop this attack with one question: did I start this sign-in on a device in front of me? If not, do not enter the code.
 Do
 Enter a device code only when a device or app in front of you, which you started yourself, is displaying it. 
 Read the sign-in prompt for the name of the app you are signing in to. Microsoft advises confirming that the prompt names the application you expect, and cancelling if it does not. 
 Check unexpected invitations and requests by another route, such as a phone call to a number you already had. 
 Report the message to your IT or security team, even when you did nothing. 
 Prefer phishing-resistant sign-in (FIDO2 keys, passkeys) where your organization offers it; Microsoft recommends this. 
 Don't
 Do not enter a code that arrived in a message, a chat or a call you did not start. 
 Do not treat a real Microsoft web address as proof that the request is real. 
 Do not approve a sign-in prompt just to make a meeting or file open. 
 Do not follow a hurry-up message that says the code expires in minutes. 
 Do not rely on a phone call as proof; callers can say anything. 
 Microsoft's own advice in the Storm-2372 write-up is the same two points: confirm that the sign-in prompt names the app you expect, and do not enter a device code you were not expecting, especially one that came in an unsolicited meeting invitation or message.
 Keeping your account safe from it
 Little of this needs software. It is mostly habit plus a few settings for the people who run accounts.
 Do
 Treat every code request you did not start as hostile. 
 Use a passkey or a security key where you can; they resist phishing better than texts or app codes. 
 Keep your work and personal accounts apart and use a password manager. 
 Ask your administrator whether device code flow is blocked in your organization. 
 Know who to tell at work before you need to. 
 Don't
 Do not rely on text message codes alone if a better method is offered. 
 Do not forward a code to anyone, including someone who claims to be support. 
 Do not leave old sessions and unknown devices listed on your account. 
 Is device code phishing dangerous? What the senders want
 The attack chain, step by step
 The diagram below shows the four steps. The point to take from it is the timing: the attacker has to send the code and have you enter it before it expires, which is why lures push hurry.
 Our own diagram of the device code phishing chain, based on Microsoft's Storm-2372 write-up and Microsoft Learn. Based on Microsoft Learn (OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant) and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (Storm-2372). Step What the attacker does What you see 
 1 Starts a device sign-in and receives a user code from Microsoft Nothing yet 
 2 Sends you the code with a reason to enter it: a meeting, a shared document, a verification, a support call A message that feels routine or urgent 
 3 Waits while Microsoft's service is polled for completion You open the real Microsoft device login page and type the code 
 4 You sign in and approve; the attacker's session is issued tokens Often a confirmation that looks harmless, or an error 
 What we checked on 1 November 2026, and what we could not
 This topic has no single website to test. Our check was a plain look at what Microsoft, news reports and security vendors have published; we ran no phishing kit and tested no account. Where a fact comes from a news report of a vendor's finding, we say so.
 Our reading of the sources, 1 November 2026
 The technique is real and documented Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its Storm-2372 write-up on 13 February 2025 and describes the campaign as active since August 2024. 
 It is not a Microsoft vulnerability Microsoft says the technique does not reflect a vulnerability in its products. 
 Who uses it Microsoft attributes Storm-2372 with moderate confidence to actors aligned with Russian interests and later assessed it as an initial access sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard (update of 31 July 2026). News reports describe other clusters and criminal kits using the same method. We cannot verify those attributions ourselves. 
 Size of the 2026 wave A March 2026 news report cites more than 340 organizations hit in five countries, and a June 2026 report cites LevelBlue saying activity peaked in May 2026. These are figures from third parties, and we did not confirm them. 
 Indicators Microsoft's write-up lists hunting signals, not addresses or file hashes. We have no list of malicious domains to give you, and we do not publish one we could not verify. 
 Stolen sessions are quiet A clean look at your mailbox does not clear an account. The attacker's access looks like an ordinary sign-in, so absence of anything odd proves little. 
 Treat an unexpected code request as an attack The method is real, documented by Microsoft and in wide use. One quiet check does not clear an account. If you entered a code you did not ask for, act as if the account is open to someone else.
 How people are lured into entering the code
 The code itself is harmless. The lure is what matters, and Microsoft documented several in the Storm-2372 campaign. Other lures come from news reports; the common thread is a reason to type a code on a Microsoft page.
 1 Rapport first, then an invitation
 Microsoft describes the actor contacting targets on messaging apps such as WhatsApp, Signal and Microsoft Teams while posing as a prominent person relevant to the target. After building trust, the actor sends an email with an invitation to an online meeting or event.
 2 A fake meeting that needs a code
 In Microsoft's account, the target is told to enter a code on the genuine Microsoft sign-in page, and the code is presented as the ID of the meeting. A real meeting ID joins a meeting; it never needs your account sign-in on a device login page.
 3 Lures that copy chat apps
 Microsoft also saw lures that emulate WhatsApp and Signal experiences. The shape is the same: a step that seems like part of joining or verifying, ending at a code box.
 4 Shared files and compromised senders
 News reports on Proofpoint's tracking of a cluster it calls UNK_AcademicFlare describe compromised email accounts and spoofed OneDrive links used against government, academic and transportation targets. A message from a colleague's hacked account is the hardest to doubt, so check unusual requests by another route.
 5 Phone calls and fake IT help
 Our reading, not something we could confirm from the pages we read: a caller who says they are from IT and asks you to enter a code to verify yourself fits the technique exactly. No real helpdesk needs you to approve a code you did not request yourself.
 How the technique spread, 2024 to 2026
 The timeline combines Microsoft's own dates with reports from news sites about vendor findings. Dates from news pages are marked as such.
 August 2024
 Storm-2372 campaign begins
 Microsoft says the device code phishing campaign it tracks as Storm-2372 has been active since this month. Targets included government, NGOs, IT services and technology, defense, telecommunications, health, higher education and energy, in Europe, North America, Africa and the Middle East.
 13 February 2025
 Microsoft publishes the write-up
 The post explains the lures, the token capture, the use of Microsoft Graph to search mail for words like password and admin, and the spread of phishing from the victim's own account. It recommends blocking the device code flow where possible.
 14 February 2025
 A persistence update
 Microsoft added that the actor switched to the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID. This gives a refresh token that can be used with the device registration service, so the actor can register a device in Entra ID, obtain a Primary Refresh Token and keep access from that device. The actor also used proxies matched to each target's region.
 December 2025
 More clusters reported
 A news report from December 2025 describes Russia-linked groups using Microsoft 365 device code phishing, naming clusters such as UTA0304, UTA0307 and UNK_AcademicFlare in addition to Storm-2372. We have not verified the attributions.
 March 2026
 A kit for sale and a large campaign
 A March 2026 news report says a campaign hit more than 340 organizations in the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Germany, with the earliest observation on 18 February 2026, and describes a phishing-as-a-service kit named EvilTokens that Sekoia says has been sold since mid-February 2026.
 May to June 2026
 Activity peaks, more kits
 A report from June 2026 cites LevelBlue as saying several kits now support the technique, including EvilTokens, Kali365, Ghost Hub, Cyb3r and Tycoon2FA, and that activity peaked in May 2026.
 31 July 2026
 Microsoft links Storm-2372 to Midnight Blizzard
 Microsoft updated its post to say it now assesses Storm-2372 as an initial access sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, based on technical and operational overlaps.
 Our own timeline, using the dates given by Microsoft and by the news reports cited in the sources. What the attacker does after you enter the code
 What follows is taken from Microsoft's description of Storm-2372. Other actors may do different things with the same access, and we do not claim that every attack looks like this.
 Source: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Storm-2372 conducts device code phishing campaign (13 February 2025, updated 14 February 2025 and 31 July 2026). Action What Microsoft reports What it means for you 
 Reads your mail Uses Microsoft Graph to search mail for keywords such as username, password, admin, teamviewer, anydesk, credentials, secret, ministry and gov, and exfiltrates matching emails Anything sensitive in your mailbox may be copied 
 Phishes your contacts Sends more phishing from the compromised account to internal users, moving sideways Colleagues receive a message that really comes from you 
 Registers a device Uses the Authentication Broker client ID to register a device in Entra ID and obtain a Primary Refresh Token Access can continue from the attacker's device after a password change 
 Hides its location Uses proxies matched to the target's region Sign-ins may look local 
 Microsoft's write-up does not describe what is done with personal Microsoft accounts. Its reporting concerns organizations, so for a home user we do not know how often the technique targets consumer accounts.
 What this can cost you
 The damage depends on what the account can reach. A work account that opens email, files and chat is a much bigger prize than an empty one, and the attacker gets all of it at once.
 High Mailbox and file access
 The tokens act with your rights. Microsoft saw attackers searching mail for credentials and remote access tool names, so a stolen mailbox can lead to more intrusions.
 High Attacks on your colleagues and contacts
 Phishing sent from your real account is far more convincing than phishing from a stranger. Microsoft describes this lateral spread.
 High Access that outlives a password change
 Refresh tokens and registered devices can keep working until sessions are revoked. A new password on its own may not remove them.
 Medium Data and legal duties for organizations
 A company may have to report a breach if personal data was in the mailbox. That is for your security and legal team to judge, not for a guide.
 Low Nothing, if you did not enter the code
 A code is useless to the attacker until a person types it on the Microsoft page. If you ignored the message, there is nothing to undo, only a message to report.
 What to do after the device code phishing e-mail
 If you only received the message and clicked nothing, step 3 is all you need.
 If you clicked the link or typed anything on the page it opened, do every step, starting with the password.
 1 Step 1 : Change the password you typed on the fake page
 If you entered a password after clicking the link in the device code phishing message, treat that account as known to the sender.
 Open the provider's real site by typing its address yourself, not through any link in the e-mail, and change the password there. Choose a new one you have never used before, and change it on every other account that shared the old one.
 Then use the option to sign out of all other sessions or devices, if the provider has one. This works the same in any browser on Windows 11 and Windows 10.
 Microsoft account, Security page (account.microsoft.com/security): Change password. Full procedure with screenshots: Turn on two-step verification / secure a hacked account 
 Get a free scan and check if your PC is infected.
 Fortect scans Windows for malware and the damage it leaves behind. It does not decrypt files.
 Remove it now To use the full-featured product, you have to purchase a license for Fortect. The scan is free. 2 Step 2 : Turn on two-step verification
 Two-step verification asks for a code from your phone or an authenticator app whenever someone signs in from a new device. A stolen password alone is then not enough to open the mailbox.
 Turn it on in the security settings of the e-mail account first, then for the bank, shop and social accounts that send their reset links to that address.
 While you are there, check the recovery e-mail and phone number and the forwarding rules, which attackers sometimes change to keep access. The settings pages look the same on Windows 11 and Windows 10.
 Microsoft account: Manage how I sign in, where two-step verification and the sign-in methods are. Full procedure with screenshots: Turn on two-step verification / secure a hacked account 
 3 Step 3 : Report the e-mail and delete it
 Report the message instead of only deleting it. In Outlook choose Report > Report phishing , in Gmail the three-dot menu > Report phishing ; the provider then blocks the same message for other people.
 Do not reply and do not click anything else in it. On a work account, forward it to your IT team as an attachment first. Web mail and the mail apps on Windows 11 and Windows 10 offer the same options.
 New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web: Report > Report phishing. Full procedure with screenshots: Report a phishing e-mail 
 4 Step 4 : Scan the PC if you opened a file from the message
 A page that only asked for a password installs nothing, so most readers can skip this step.
 If the device code phishing e-mail or the page it opened made you download or open a file, delete it and run a full scan, then a Microsoft Defender Offline scan.
 In Windows 11 and Windows 10 open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Scan options , select Microsoft Defender Antivirus (offline scan) and click Scan now . The PC restarts and the scan takes about 15 minutes, so save your work first.
 Windows 11: Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Scan options. Full procedure with screenshots: Run a Microsoft Defender Offline scan 
 Did the manual steps not help?
 Get a free scan and check if your PC is infected. Fortect scans Windows for malware, unwanted programs and the Windows damage they leave behind.
 Remove it now To use the full-featured product, you have to purchase a license for Fortect. The scan is free. If you already entered a code: what to do, in order
 Act at once. We could not read a Microsoft page that gives step by step screens for ordinary users, so we give the order of actions and name the settings only in general terms. Your IT team will have the exact tools.
 1 Tell your IT or security team first
 If the account is a work or school account, report it now and say the time you entered the code. Microsoft says users should report suspicious activity so it can be investigated and tokens revoked. Do not wait to see whether anything happens.
 2 Ask them to revoke sessions
 Microsoft's incident response advice is to revoke refresh tokens, which administrators can do with the revokeSignInSessions call in Microsoft Graph, and to consider a Conditional Access policy that forces everyone to sign in again. This is what ends the attacker's access; it is an administrator task.
 3 Have them check sign-ins and devices
 Microsoft names these signals for responders: risky sign-ins, anonymous IP activity, error code 50199 followed by a success within minutes, anomalous mail reads through Graph, and newly registered devices in Entra ID close to unusual token activity.
 4 Then change your password and sign in again
 Change the password from a device you trust, not one the attacker may control, and register your second factor again if told to. Do this after sessions are revoked, since a password change alone may leave tokens alive.
 5 Warn the people you write to
 Tell colleagues and contacts to be careful with messages from you since the time you entered the code, because the account may have sent phishing.
 6 If it is a personal account
 There is no administrator, so use your account's security settings to change the password, review recent sign-in activity and sign out of all devices. We could not read a Microsoft page with the exact screens, so look for these options in your account's security area rather than relying on a path from us. Turn on a stronger second factor, such as an authenticator app or a passkey.
 7 Scan the device you used, as a precaution
 Device code phishing does not put a program on your computer, so a scan will not undo it. A scan is still sensible if the same message also pushed a download. The account steps above are what close this attack.
 Our own checklist of the order of actions, from Microsoft's incident response advice. For administrators: limit or block the device code flow
 Microsoft recommends getting as close as possible to a unilateral block on the device code flow, and allowing it only in well documented, secured uses such as legacy tooling that cannot be updated.
 1 Audit first
 Microsoft suggests a policy that audits current use of the flow so you can learn whether anything still needs it before you block it.
 2 Create the Conditional Access policy
 Microsoft Learn describes this path: sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center as at least a Conditional Access Administrator, go to Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies and choose New policy . Under Conditions > Authentication Flows set Configure to Yes and select Device code flow . Under Access controls > Grant choose Block access .
 3 Exclude emergency accounts, start in report-only
 Exclude your emergency access (break-glass) accounts and any other required users, and audit that list regularly. Set the policy to Report-only first, review the results, then move Enable policy to On .
 4 Strengthen the rest
 Microsoft also recommends requiring MFA, preferring phishing-resistant methods, blocking legacy authentication, using sign-in risk policies, restricting who can register devices in Entra ID and reviewing risky sign-in reports.
 5 Hunt
 Microsoft describes Defender XDR hunting queries that correlate clicks on devicelogin URLs, risky sign-ins and error code 50199 followed by success, plus a query for new device registrations.
 Names that sound the same, and are not
 Several searches land on this page by mistake, so here is what is and is not the same thing.
 Our reading of the terms; only the device authorization grant and Storm-2372 points come from Microsoft's pages. Term What it is Same as device code phishing? 
 Fake login page (credential phishing) A copy of a sign-in page that records the password you type No. Here the page is real and no password is typed into a fake one 
 Adversary in the middle phishing A proxy that sits between you and the real site and captures the session No, but the result is similar: a stolen session 
 Consent phishing A malicious app asks you to grant it permissions Related but different mechanism 
 Quishing Phishing through a QR code No, though a lure can use a QR code to reach the code page 
 A real device sign-in on a TV or printer You start it on the device, and it shows you a code No. This is the legitimate use of the same feature 
 Questions about device code phishing
 What is device code phishing?
 Device code phishing is a scam in which an attacker starts a sign-in on their own machine, receives a short code from Microsoft and tricks you into typing it on the real Microsoft device login page. 
 When you sign in and pass the second factor, Microsoft approves the attacker's session, and they receive access and refresh tokens for your account without ever learning your password.
 Microsoft describes it in its February 2025 write-up on Storm-2372 and says it is a misuse of a feature, not a vulnerability. Nothing is installed on your computer, so the account is what needs protecting.
 Is device code phishing dangerous?
 Yes, for the account it targets. The attacker acts with your rights, and Microsoft saw them searching mail for words like password, admin and credentials, copying matching emails and sending more phishing from the victim's account to colleagues.
 Microsoft also reported a way of registering a device in Entra ID so that access can continue from that device. The danger is much lower if you never enter the code. A code that nobody types does nothing, so ignoring the message and reporting it ends the risk.
 How does the attack get past multi-factor authentication?
 It does not break MFA; it uses it. You complete the password and second factor yourself, on the genuine Microsoft page, but the sign-in you approve belongs to the attacker's session, because that is the session the code was issued for.
 Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 keys or Microsoft Authenticator with passkeys, and advises against telephony-based MFA. Even those methods do not help if you approve the wrong request, so the habit of not entering codes you did not start matters most.
 I entered a code. What should I do now?
 Tell your IT or security team at once if it is a work or school account, and say when you entered the code. Microsoft's incident response advice is to revoke refresh tokens, which an administrator can do, and to consider forcing everyone to sign in again.
 After that, change your password from a trusted device, re-register your second factor if asked, and warn contacts who may get mail from your account. A password change alone may leave the attacker's tokens working, so do not stop there.
 Will changing my password stop the attacker?
 Not by itself. The attacker holds tokens, and Microsoft says a refresh token can keep producing new access tokens. In its update of 14 February 2025 Microsoft also described the actor registering a device in Entra ID to obtain a Primary Refresh Token, which lets access continue from that device.
 The sessions need to be revoked and unknown devices removed by an administrator. Change the password as well, but do it after the sessions are revoked, from a device you trust.
 Is microsoft.com/devicelogin a scam?
 No. The device login page is a real Microsoft page used for legitimate sign-ins on devices such as TVs and printers, where you start the sign-in yourself and the device shows you the code. The page is not the problem.
 The problem is entering a code that someone else gave you. Our check cannot tell you whether a given message is genuine, so use one rule: type a code only if a device in front of you, which you started, is showing it.
 Can an antivirus find or remove device code phishing?
 No, because no malware is installed. The attack lives in the account, in the tokens the attacker holds. A scan of your computer will not remove them.
 What helps is revoking the sign-in sessions, checking sign-ins and registered devices, and changing credentials. A scan is a reasonable precaution only if the same message also pushed a download. Microsoft says Defender for Office 365 can detect the malicious emails and Entra ID Protection can raise risk detections for suspicious sign-ins, but those are tools for organizations.
 How can a company block device code phishing?
 Microsoft recommends blocking the device code flow where possible, with a Conditional Access policy. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, create a policy that targets the Authentication Flows condition, selects Device code flow and blocks access, excluding emergency accounts.
 Start in report-only mode, review the effect, then turn it on. Where the flow is still needed, allow it only through narrow policies. Add MFA with phishing-resistant methods, sign-in risk policies and limits on who can register devices.
 Who is behind device code phishing attacks?
 More than one group. Microsoft attributes Storm-2372 with moderate confidence to actors aligned with Russian interests and, in a July 2026 update, assesses it as an initial access sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard.
 News reports name other clusters and say phishing kits such as EvilTokens, sold since mid-February 2026, put the method in reach of criminals. We have not verified those attributions ourselves, so treat them as the vendors' findings, not ours.
 Will Fortect remove device code phishing?
 Fortect scans Windows for malware and unwanted programs and repairs the system files and settings they change, and its free scan shows what it finds on your PC before you decide anything. 
 For device code phishing, follow the plan above as well: the browser steps take back permissions and settings that no scanner treats as a threat, and uninstalling the program that brought it removes the source.
 Run Microsoft Defender's full scan and, if anything was found, its offline scan as a second opinion. If the symptoms are gone after the plan and both scans are clean, there is nothing more to do.
